turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Hi, come on in and have a seat. I'm Dr. Adiz Akonquo, one of the cardiologists here. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thomas Weixerec, August 3rd, 1964.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Thank you, Mr.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Weixerec.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Did you find parking okay? The garage is a mess this week with the construction.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Took me two laps, but yeah, I found a spot eventually.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Sorry about that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So, Dr.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Patel sent you over about some chest discomfort. Tell me what's been going on.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So about six weeks ago I started getting this pressure in the middle of my chest like somebody sitting on me. It happens when I walk up the hill to my house or when I carry groceries up the stairs.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: And how long does it last when it comes on? A few minutes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: If I stop and stand there it goes away in maybe three, four minutes. Does it ever happen when you're resting?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Or wake you up at night?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, never at rest. Only when I'm pushing it. Does the pressure go anywhere?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Like your arm, your jaw, or your back?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sometimes a little into my left arm. Not the jaw. Any shortness of breath with it?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: A little winded, yeah.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: But I figured that's just me being out of shape.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Any sweating,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: nausea, or lightheadedness with the episodes? No sweating, no nausea. I've never passed out or anything like that.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Has it been getting more frequent or easier to bring on? Um, not really.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's about the same, maybe two or three times a week.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Okay, doctor. Patel's note says you have high blood pressure and high cholesterol. What are you taking for those?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lisinopril 20 milligrams in the morning and he started me on adorvastatin 40 milligrams at night about a year ago any allergies to medications penicillin I got hives from it as a kid do you smoke I quit 10 years ago before that I smoked about a pack a day for 25 years good for you on quitting that's a big deal Any diabetes? No, my sugar's always been fine.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: And what do you do for work?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm a dispatcher at Hollister Freight, mostly sitting, honestly.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Okay, your blood pressure today is 142 over 86, pulse 74, and your oxygen is 98%. Weight is 214 pounds.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Let me take a listen.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Heart has a regular rhythm, no murmurs. Lungs are clear. No swelling in your legs, and the pulses in your feet are good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's good, I guess.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: We did an ECG when you came in. It shows normal sinus rhythm at 72, and I don't see any signs of an old heart attack or any acute changes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's reassuring,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: but a resting ECG is often normal even when there's a blockage, because the problem only shows up when the heart is working hard.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So what does that mean then? What you're describing,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: pressure with exertion that goes away with rest, is pretty classic for stable angina. That means the heart muscle isn't getting enough blood when it works harder, usually from narrowing in the heart arteries. With your smoking history, blood pressure and cholesterol, that's my main concern.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, that's kind of scary.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I understand. The good news is it's stable, and we have a clear plan. First, I'd like you to have a nuclear stress test where you walk on a treadmill while we take pictures of the blood flow to your heart. We'll also check a fasting lipid panel and a basic metabolic panel.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sure, that's fine.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: In the meantime, I want you to start aspirin, 81 milligrams once a day. I'm also starting Metaprolol 6 and 8, 25 milligrams once a day, which slows the heart down so it doesn't work as hard. And I'm giving you nitroglycerin, 0 .4 milligrams, one tablet under the tongue if the pressure comes on and doesn't go away with rest. You can repeat it every five minutes up to three tablets.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Got it.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'm also going to increase your adorvastatin from 40 to 80 milligrams at night. Keep the lisinopril the same.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay. Now this part is important. If you get chest pain at rest,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: or pain that lasts more than 15 minutes, or it doesn't go away after 1 nitroglycerin, call 911. Don't drive yourself.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Understood.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: And hold off on heavy lifting, and that hill, until we have the stress test results.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What's the best number to reach you for scheduling? Mycel 555 -0163.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Great. We'll get the stress test done within the next two weeks, and I'll see you back right after to go over the results.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thanks, doctor. I appreciate it.
